title: Kraft's Inequality
content: Kraft's inequality characterizes the set of achievable codeword lengths for prefix-free (instantaneous) binary codes. A set of lengths $(l_1, \ldots, l_n)$ can be realized as a prefix-free code if and only if $\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{-l_i} \le 1$. The formalization represents the implicit distribution $q_i = 2^{-l_i}$ using the equivalent form $(2^{-1})^{l_i}$.

title: Average Code Length
content: The expected code length under probability distribution $p$. This is the quantity that Huffman coding minimizes. For a code used to compress i.i.d. source symbols, $L$ determines the asymptotic compression ratio: $L$ bits per source symbol on average.

title: Optimal Code Definition
content: A code is optimal if it satisfies Kraft's inequality and no other Kraft-valid code achieves a lower average code length. This universal quantification over all alternative codes makes optimality a strong property — the Huffman algorithm is the canonical constructive witness.
mathContext: $\text{IsOptimal}(p, l) \iff \text{KraftValid}(l) \wedge \forall l',\; \text{KraftValid}(l') \Rightarrow L(p, l) \le L(p, l')$

title: Pointwise KL Divergence Bound
content: The workhorse inequality: for positive reals $p, q$, we have $p \ln(p/q) \ge p - q$. This follows from the concavity of the logarithm, specifically $\ln(x) \le x - 1$ applied to $x = q/p$. Summing over all symbols and using Kraft's inequality converts this pointwise bound into the entropy lower bound on code length. This is essentially the proof that KL divergence $D(p \| q) \ge 0$ (Gibbs' inequality).

title: Positivity of Kraft Terms
content: Each implicit probability $q_i = 2^{-l_i}$ is strictly positive, which is required to apply the KL divergence bound. This is immediate since $2^{-1} > 0$ and positive reals are closed under exponentiation.

title: Logarithm of Kraft Terms
content: Rewrites $\ln(2^{-l}) = -l \cdot \ln 2$ using the power rule for logarithms and the identity $\ln(x^{-1}) = -\ln(x)$. This algebraic step bridges the gap between the code length $l$ appearing in the average code length and the logarithmic terms in the entropy.

title: Entropy Lower Bound on Code Length
content: The central theorem: no prefix-free binary code can achieve average code length below $H(p)/\ln 2$ bits. The proof introduces the implicit distribution $r_i = 2^{-l_i}$ and applies the pointwise KL bound $p_i \ln(p_i / r_i) \ge p_i - r_i$ to each symbol. Summing and using Kraft's inequality $\sum r_i \le 1$ gives $\sum p_i \ln(p_i / r_i) \ge 0$. Expanding the logarithm yields $L \cdot \ln 2 \ge H(p)$. This is the converse direction of Shannon's source coding theorem: entropy is not just achievable, it is a genuine lower bound.

title: Entropy Non-negativity
content: Shannon entropy is non-negative for any distribution supported on $[0,1]$. Since $0 < p_i \le 1$ implies $\ln(p_i) \le 0$, each term $-p_i \ln(p_i) \ge 0$, and the sum is non-negative. This confirms that the entropy lower bound is meaningful: the minimum average code length is always at least zero.

title: Shannon Code Length
content: Shannon's coding scheme assigns symbol $i$ a codeword of length $l_i = \lceil -\log_2(p_i) \rceil$. Since $-\log_2(p_i)$ is the ideal code length (information content of symbol $i$), rounding up to the nearest integer gives a valid prefix-free code. The formalization uses natural number ceiling $\lceil \cdot \rceil_+$ and natural logarithm, computing $\lceil -\ln(p_i) / \ln 2 \rceil_+$.

title: Shannon Code Satisfies Kraft's Inequality
content: The key insight is that $2^{-l_i} \le p_i$ for each symbol: since $l_i = \lceil \log_2(1/p_i) \rceil \ge \log_2(1/p_i)$, we get $2^{-l_i} \le 2^{-\log_2(1/p_i)} = p_i$. Therefore $\sum 2^{-l_i} \le \sum p_i = 1$. The formalization converts the ceiling inequality to a logarithmic inequality, then uses $\exp$ monotonicity to lift it to the value level. This is the constructive content: Shannon coding produces a valid prefix-free code.

title: Shannon Coding Upper Bound
content: Shannon coding achieves average code length within 1 bit of the entropy: $L_S < H_2(p) + 1$, or equivalently $L_S \cdot \ln 2 < H(p) + \ln 2$. The proof uses the ceiling bound $\lceil x \rceil < x + 1$ for $x \ge 0$, applied to each symbol's ideal code length. The strict inequality requires the alphabet to be nonempty ($n > 0$). This gap of at most 1 bit per symbol can be reduced to $1/k$ bits by coding blocks of $k$ symbols — the content of Shannon's source coding theorem.

title: Optimal Code Monotonicity (Exchange Argument)
content: In any optimal prefix-free code, more probable symbols receive shorter or equal codewords. The proof is by contradiction via the exchange argument: if $p_i > p_j$ but $l_i > l_j$, swapping the codewords (lengths) of symbols $i$ and $j$ leaves the Kraft sum unchanged yet strictly reduces the average code length by $(p_i - p_j)(l_i - l_j) > 0$, contradicting optimality. This structural property is essential for the Huffman construction. It is fully formalized here: the swap is realized as a double `Function.update`, Kraft-validity is preserved via `Finset.sum_equiv` over `Equiv.swap i j`, and the strict decrease is reduced to the two affected terms.

title: Huffman Optimality (Axiomatized)
content: Huffman's 1952 theorem: among all prefix-free binary codes, the Huffman code achieves minimum average codeword length. The proof proceeds by strong induction on the alphabet size $n$. The base case $n=2$ is immediate (both symbols get length-1 codewords). For the inductive step, the monotonicity axiom places the two least probable symbols at maximum depth. Merging them into a super-symbol reduces the problem to $n-1$ symbols, where the inductive hypothesis applies. This is axiomatized because full formalization requires the Huffman tree data structure and the merge/unmerge correspondence.

title: Tight Bounds on Optimal Code Length
content: The capstone corollary combining all preceding results: the optimal code length is sandwiched as $H(p)/\ln 2 \le L^* < H(p)/\ln 2 + 1$. The lower bound comes from the entropy theorem (no code beats entropy), and the upper bound from optimality ($L^* \le L_S$) combined with the Shannon coding bound ($L_S < H_2 + 1$). This sandwich shows that entropy in bits, $H_2(p)$, characterizes the optimal compression rate to within a single bit — the quantitative content of Shannon's source coding theorem for prefix-free codes.
